title: 1966 Palomares B-52 crash
summary: A B-52G bomber collided with a KC-135 tanker during mid-air refueling at 31,000 feet over the Mediterranean Sea near Palomares, Spain. The refueling boom struck the top of the B-52 fuselage, breaking the left wing. The collision destroyed the tanker completely and caused the bomber to break apart. Four B28FI thermonuclear bombs fell, three on land and one in the sea. The bomber loss of 4 crew members plus the tanker loss of 3 crew members resulted in 7 deaths, with 4 bomber crew members successfully parachuting to safety.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from a collision during mid-air refueling when the KC-135 tanker's refueling boom struck the top of the B-52 fuselage. The B-52 pilot later reported that the collision occurred as he was following standard refueling procedures. The exact cause of the boom strike was not explicitly stated in available investigation materials, but the structural failure from the impact was catastrophic, resulting in separation of the left wing and breakup of both aircraft.

factors.evidence: The refueling boom of the KC-135 struck the top of the B-52 fuselage, breaking a longeron and snapping off the left wing, resulting in an explosion witnessed by a second B-52 about one mile away.
The nozzle of the refueling boom made contact with the fuselage during refueling operations, a collision between the two aircraft in flight.
The impact broke a longeron and snapped off the left wing of the B-52, causing an explosion and immediate loss of control of both aircraft.
The refueling boom design and the geometry of the contact point between boom and fuselage allowed a single impact to cause catastrophic structural damage.

B-52G lost control; three crew members killed: navigator First Lieutenant Steven G. Montanus, electronic warfare officer First Lieutenant George J. Glessner, and gunner Technical Sergeant Ronald P. Snyder unable to eject. Four surviving crew members parachuted to safety.

notes: Four B28FI Mod 2 Y1 thermonuclear bombs aboard the B-52; three fell on land near Palomares with conventional explosives detonating and dispersing plutonium over 2 km² of terrain.

Part of Operation Chrome Dome, a Cold War continuous airborne alert mission with nuclear-armed bombers.

title: Lufthansa 005
summary: Lufthansa Flight 005 was on final approach to Bremen in fog, heavy rain, and darkness with a 6-knot tailwind exceeding the 5-knot maximum. An instrument displayed false information causing the aircraft to deviate from the ILS glide path. The captain estimated altitude incorrectly during the transition from instruments to visual control. At approximately 10 meters above ground, the captain commenced a go-around but maneuvered the aircraft into an extreme flight attitude causing a stall. The aircraft spun left, struck the ground with its left wing, and crashed 400 meters beyond the runway end.

The captain's altitude estimate was incorrect due to darkness and poor visibility. title: PIA 17
summary: Pakistan International Airlines Flight 17, a Sikorsky S-61N helicopter, crashed near Faridpur on February 2, 1966, while on final approach to its heliport, killing all 3 crew members and 20 of 21 passengers. An oil leak developed from an external pipe connected to the main gearbox 15 minutes after takeoff. One of the retreating blades was struck by a vulture en route, but the flight continued normally until the main transmission lost power despite both engines running normally.

The rear sleeve bearing failure was caused by an oil leak, although the source of the leak was not established due to destruction by fire.

title: Canadian Pacific Air Lines 402
summary: Flight 402, a DC-8-43 flying Hong Kong-Tokyo-Vancouver, held near Haneda for 38 minutes and cancelled one approach as visibility fluctuated below minima at night. After diverting toward Taipei and being told visibility had improved to a 3,000 ft runway visual range, the captain flew a second approach; advised the aircraft was 20 ft low near the runway, it continued below and parallel to the glide slope before a sharp descent struck eleven approach lights and the seawall short of the threshold. The pilot lost control after impact and 64 of 72 aboard were killed. Investigators found no tower fault, attributing the crash to pilot error and possible optical illusion from poor visibility.

title: LANSA 501
summary: Flight 501 departed Lima at 07:40 AM and climbed on a heading of 190° until reaching 9 nm southwest of the airport, then turned toward Cusco. The crew violated the planned route by flying a direct straight route toward the mountain range. Eyewitnesses reported the aircraft flying low over San Pedro de Pilas at 8:00 AM at a heading of 100° and turning left to avoid mountains. The aircraft struck Mount Talaula around 08:05 AM at approximately the planned deviation point.
probable_cause: The crew violated the planned route regulations and flew a straight course toward Cusco, becoming unable to clear the summits due to insufficient climb performance. The captain may have overestimated the aircraft's technical abilities, with his judgment impaired by lack of rest and pre-flight preparation.

factors.evidence: The crew violated the planned route regulations provided by the airline and decided to fly a straight route from Las Palmas to Cusco instead of the prescribed routing.

The captain had completed the previous day's duties late, it was assumed he had a rest period of only 6½ hours before the flight.
Flight 501 struck Mount Talaula around 8:05 AM PET, with the wreckage being recovered the next day and all 49 occupants killed.

title: Britannia Airways 105

title: All Nippon Airways 533
summary: ANA Flight 533 approached Matsuyama airport in an unstable state higher than normal and executed a long landing 460 meters beyond the runway threshold. The crew initiated a go-around but lost control at 70 to 100 meters altitude and crashed into the Seto Inland Sea. The cause of the accident was never determined.

title: Pan Am 708
summary: A Pan Am Boeing 727 cargo flight crashed on initial approach less than 10 miles west-southwest of Berlin Tegel in the early morning of November 15, 1966. The flight encountered poor weather with snow. The cause was undetermined because US investigators were not allowed to survey the impact site at a Soviet military training ground and only half of the aircraft remains were returned by Soviet authorities.

title: 1966 Flying Tiger Line Canadair CL-44 crash
summary: A Flying Tiger Line Canadair CL-44 carrying munitions for the US Air Force approached Da Nang Airport on December 24, 1966 in rain and foggy conditions with critically low fuel reserves. The crew continued the approach below the glide path and the aircraft struck trees at a kilometer south of the runway, crashing into Binh Thai village. All four crew members and 107 people on the ground were killed.
probable_cause: The crew continued the approach under the glide path, probably due to the poor weather conditions during the flight. The low fuel state made aborting the landing impossible.
